iterators-generators.summary: Know the difference between iterables and single-pass iterators, how generators pause and resume (including send, throw and close), and how the with statement and contextlib guarantee cleanup.
points: An iterable produces iterators via `__iter__`; an iterator also has `__next__` and is used up after one pass. map, zip, filter, generators and files are iterators; lists, ranges and dict views are not.

Calling a generator function runs nothing. `next()` runs to the next `yield`; `send(v)` makes the paused `yield` evaluate to `v` (prime with `next()` first); `throw()` raises at the `yield`; `close()` raises GeneratorExit there.
A generator's `return value` becomes `StopIteration.value`, and `yield from` evaluates to it. `yield from` also forwards send, throw and close to the subgenerator.
In a generator expression only the outermost iterable is evaluated at creation; conditions and inner loops run lazily and see later rebindings.
`with` calls `__enter__` (its return is bound by `as`) and always calls `__exit__`; a truthy return from `__exit__` suppresses the exception. Multiple managers exit in reverse order.
With `@contextmanager`, the body's exception is raised at the `yield`: wrap it in try/finally for cleanup, and yield exactly once.
Since PEP 479, a StopIteration leaking out of a generator body becomes RuntimeError; use `next(it, default)` instead.
traps: `x in gen`, `zip(it, it)` and `takewhile` all consume items you may expect to still be there.
Yielding inside `finally` or `except GeneratorExit` makes `close()` raise "generator ignored GeneratorExit".
Breaking out of `async for` does not close the async generator immediately; use `contextlib.aclosing()` for deterministic cleanup.
